descriptor: Matching set (elements): identify which element has marine sediments forming limestone as a major long-term sink.
solution: Limestone is calcium carbonate built from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, so seafloor sediment locks away carbon for geologic time. The keyed element is carbon; the other listed elements are not stored mainly as carbonate rock.

descriptor: Matching set (elements): which element is commercially obtained from seabird guano deposits.
solution: Seabird droppings from fish-eating birds are rich in phosphate because phosphorus moves up the food chain from fish. Guano is mined as fertilizer, so the keyed element is phosphorus.

descriptor: Matching set (elements): which element in the mineral pyrite drives acid mine drainage.
solution: Pyrite is iron sulfide. When mining exposes it to air and water, the sulfur oxidizes and forms sulfuric acid that leaches into streams. The keyed element is sulfur.

descriptor: Matching set (laws and treaties): which one requires federal agencies to prepare an environmental impact statement for government-funded projects.
solution: The National Environmental Policy Act is the law that requires an environmental impact statement before major federal actions. The other choices protect species, regulate emissions or ozone-depleting chemicals, or set aside wilderness.
notes: Specific US statute (NEPA) is not itemized in the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Matching set (laws and treaties): which one includes a provision allowing private landowners to alter land under a habitat conservation plan.
solution: Habitat conservation plans are a provision of the Endangered Species Act: a landowner agrees to offset harm to a listed species and, in return, may develop part of the property. The other listed measures contain no such provision.

descriptor: Matching set (laws and treaties): which agreement addressed stratospheric ozone depletion.
solution: The Montreal Protocol committed nations to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and related ozone-depleting chemicals. Kyoto addressed greenhouse gases rather than ozone.

descriptor: Matching set (energy sources): which source has noise and release of corrosive chemicals as drawbacks.
solution: Geothermal plants bring hot fluid up from underground, and that fluid can carry dissolved salts and gases that corrode equipment and must be handled. Steam release also makes noise. The other sources lack this combination.

descriptor: Matching set (energy sources): which source is used more in the least developed countries than in highly developed ones.
solution: Biomass, mainly wood, charcoal and dung burned for cooking and heat, is the main fuel for many poor households. Wealthier countries rely far more on fossil fuels, nuclear and large hydropower.

descriptor: Matching set (energy sources): which source converts sunlight directly into electricity.
solution: Photovoltaic cells use the photoelectric effect in semiconductors to turn light into an electric current with no heat engine in between. Biomass and hydropower store solar energy indirectly.

descriptor: Choose, from five population-versus-time graphs, the one for growth at biotic potential.
solution: Biotic potential is the maximum growth rate with unlimited resources, which gives exponential growth: a curve that bends steadily upward. The keyed graph is the J-shaped curve. A straight rising line would be linear growth, not exponential.

descriptor: Choose, from the same five graphs, the one for a population that grew and then leveled off at carrying capacity.
solution: A population limited by resources rises quickly and then flattens at the carrying capacity, producing the S-shaped (logistic) curve. The keyed graph levels off at a plateau.

descriptor: Ocean cross-section with five depth zones: identify the zone with the greatest biodiversity.
solution: The keyed zone is the shallow nearshore area at the water's edge, where light, nutrients and varied habitat support the richest variety of life. Deeper zones have fewer niches because of darkness and pressure.
notes: Figure rendered; zone labels read from the diagram; keyed answer accepted as printed.

descriptor: Same ocean cross-section: which zone has species adapted to the least light and highest pressure.
solution: Light vanishes with depth and pressure rises about one atmosphere per 10 m, so the deepest zone holds organisms adapted to darkness and extreme pressure.

descriptor: Same ocean cross-section: which zone absorbs the greatest total mass of CO2 from the atmosphere.
solution: CO2 uptake in the ocean is dominated by phytoplankton photosynthesis in the sunlit surface layer over the continental shelf and open water. The large area of this lit zone gives the biggest total uptake.

descriptor: Which health outcome is NOT a likely consequence of indoor air pollution (asthma, lung cancer, skin cancer, flu-like symptoms, respiratory disease).
solution: Indoor pollutants such as radon, smoke, mold and volatile chemicals harm the lungs and cause headaches and fatigue. Skin cancer comes from ultraviolet exposure, not from indoor air, so it is the exception.

descriptor: Calculation: a 2.0 W clock runs 8,600 hours a year; find annual energy use in kWh.
solution: Energy = power × time = 2.0 W × 8,600 h = 17,200 Wh. Dividing by 1,000 gives 17.2 kWh, closest to 17.

descriptor: What is the main purpose of photosynthesis for a primary producer: oxygen, CO2, glucose, protein or water.
solution: Producers use light to convert CO2 and water into glucose, the energy-rich sugar that fuels their metabolism and builds biomass. Oxygen is a by-product, not the goal.

descriptor: Which ecosystem has the lowest net primary productivity per square meter per year: taiga, open ocean, temperate grassland, estuary, farmland.
solution: Open ocean has very few nutrients, so productivity per unit area is low even though its total area is huge. Estuaries and farmland are nutrient-rich and far more productive per square meter.

descriptor: Which is NOT a property of water (melting and boiling points, biological use, density at 4 °C versus 20 °C, heat absorbed during vaporization).
solution: Water has a very high heat of vaporization, so it absorbs a large amount of heat when it evaporates. Saying it absorbs relatively little heat is false; the other statements are true.
notes: Physical properties of water are not itemized in the 2026 CED; scope judged from topic list.

descriptor: Best evidence that the Aswan High Dam was an ecological disaster (archaeological flooding, sardines, power supply, upstream diversion, trapped silt).
solution: The dam traps nutrient-rich sediment that once fertilized the floodplain and fed the delta's fisheries. Loss of that silt is an ecological harm; power supply is a benefit, and the other options are not ecological evidence.

descriptor: Bar graph of bird and mammal extinctions by century: how many more mammal extinctions occurred in 1901-2000 than 1801-1900.
solution: Reading the bars, mammal extinctions were about 135 in the last century and about 50 the century before. The difference is roughly 85 to 90, so the choice of 90 fits.

descriptor: Most likely reason the most bird extinctions occurred in 1901-2000.
solution: Human land clearing, hunting, pollution and introduced species altered or destroyed habitats at an increasing rate. The other options describe changes that did not drive the twentieth-century rise.

descriptor: Which best describes acid mine drainage.
solution: Water that flows through exposed sulfide minerals in coal or metal mines becomes acidic and carries toxic metals into streams. It is leakage of that contaminated water, not an acid-based mining method or a result of acid rain.

descriptor: Which is a characteristic of tropical rain forests (low rainfall, high soil pH, nutrient-poor soils, low diversity, rain shadows).
solution: Most nutrients in a rain forest are held in living biomass because heavy rain and rapid decomposition leave little in the soil. The soils are thin and nutrient-poor, even though diversity and rainfall are very high.

descriptor: Which best characterizes exponential population growth.
solution: Exponential growth means a constant percentage increase per time period, so the population doubles after equal time intervals. Equal numeric increases would describe linear growth.

descriptor: Which switch from large-scale conventional farming most reduces farmworker and neighbor exposure to toxic chemicals.
solution: Integrated pest management relies on monitoring, biological control and targeted use, so far less pesticide is applied. No-till, contour plowing and cover crops protect soil but do not primarily reduce chemical exposure, and crop dusting increases it.

descriptor: Which action best illustrates a climate-change mitigation approach.
solution: Mitigation reduces the cause by cutting greenhouse-gas emissions. Replacing fossil-fuel electricity with wind power does so. More air conditioners adapt to heat, and cheaper fuel or coal power would raise emissions.

descriptor: Which component of photochemical smog is a reddish-brown, pungent gas.
solution: Nitrogen dioxide is the reddish-brown gas formed from vehicle and combustion emissions, and sunlight drives its reactions to form ozone. Ozone, CO and methane are colorless.

descriptor: A large sewage spill into a river most likely causes a sharp what.
solution: Organic waste feeds decomposers, which consume dissolved oxygen, so biochemical oxygen demand rises. Dissolved oxygen then falls and oxygen-sensitive fish decline, and coliform counts rise.

descriptor: Which statement about invasive exotic species is FALSE.
solution: Invasive species typically succeed because they reproduce quickly, which means high, not low, reproductive rates. The other statements about competition, predation, human introduction and variety of taxa are true.

descriptor: Which is the best example of gray water.
solution: Gray water is wastewater from sinks, showers and laundry, which has no toilet waste and can be reused for irrigation. Toilet and garbage-disposal water is black water.

descriptor: Global warming is likely to cause all of these EXCEPT which one (ice sheet, plant range, insects, UV radiation, sea level).
solution: Warming shrinks ice sheets, shifts plant ranges, boosts insect numbers and raises sea level. Ground-level ultraviolet radiation depends on stratospheric ozone, not on greenhouse warming.

descriptor: Rats showed steadily increasing effects as toxin concentration rose; what does this suggest.
solution: A steady rise in effect with dose is a linear dose-response relationship. A threshold would show no effect up to a certain dose, which the steady increase does not suggest.

descriptor: Energy-flow diagram of the greenhouse effect: units contributed by greenhouse gases.
solution: In the diagram the gases absorb surface infrared and re-emit about 60 units back down toward the surface; this return flow is their greenhouse contribution. The other values in the diagram belong to different flows, such as the 70 units escaping to space or the 120 units radiated from the surface.
notes: Diagram read; values consistent with key.

descriptor: Same diagram: units of energy absorbed by Earth's surface.
solution: The surface absorbs 50 units of sunlight plus 70 units of infrared returned from the atmosphere, for 120 units. That matches the 120 units it radiates upward.

descriptor: Same diagram: units of energy returned to space from Earth and atmosphere.
solution: Outgoing energy balances incoming: 30 units of reflected sunlight plus 70 units of emitted infrared make 100 units, equal to the 100 arriving.

descriptor: Population momentum is most likely when a large share of people are in which age group.
solution: Momentum occurs when many people are younger than reproductive age, because they will have children soon and the population keeps growing even if fertility drops. Older groups do not produce this effect.

descriptor: Which pair of statistics most likely indicates the highest quality of life.
solution: High life expectancy and low infant mortality reflect good health care, nutrition and sanitation. The other pairs each pair a favorable with an unfavorable indicator.

descriptor: Which action most likely reduces US contribution to rising atmospheric CO2 (organic farming, stop logging, oil to coal heating, cars to rail, ozone protection).
solution: Rail moves people and freight using much less fuel per unit than road vehicles, so fossil-fuel CO2 falls. Burning coal for heat raises emissions, and ozone protection concerns UV, not CO2.

descriptor: Persistent estrogen-mimicking chemicals such as PCBs would most affect which group.
solution: Persistent chemicals biomagnify, so concentrations are highest in higher trophic levels. Secondary consumers carry larger doses than producers or decomposers, and hormone mimics disrupt their reproduction.

descriptor: Correct statements about the northern spotted owl (pioneer species, old-growth habitat, top carnivore).
solution: The owl needs mature old-growth forest and feeds at a high trophic level on small mammals. It is not a pioneer or opportunistic species, so only statements II and III hold.
notes: Species-specific case study not required by the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Item 42 appears as a deleted slot; the booklet prints only a note that it was not scored.
solution: No solution is possible: the item text is not printed in this copy and the answer key marks it as not used in scoring.
notes: Item 42 was not scored and its question text is absent from the source; unit/topic are placeholders.

descriptor: Which compound is NOT involved in stratospheric ozone depletion.
solution: Chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds release atoms that destroy ozone. Carbon dioxide has neither and affects climate, not ozone.

descriptor: Which greenhouse gas comes only from human sources.
solution: Chlorofluorocarbons are synthetic chemicals that never occurred naturally. Nitrous oxide, CO2 and methane have natural sources as well.

descriptor: Country with negligible migration: birth rate fell from 44 to 16 and death rate from 17 to 5; what stage is it in.
solution: Both rates are falling and births are far above deaths, with net growth about 11 per thousand, which is still positive. That pattern is the industrial stage, since birth rates have fallen but remain above death rates.
notes: Item text says the same data; solution computes natural increase 16 minus 5 per thousand per year.

descriptor: Why are decomposers in soil and water important to ecosystems.
solution: Decomposers break dead matter into simple inorganic nutrients that producers can take up again. This recycling keeps nutrients cycling and is the essential service they provide.

descriptor: Pond pH fell from 8.2 to 5.2 over fifty years; which other changes are expected (oxygen, heavy metals, fish species).
solution: Acidification mobilizes aluminum and other heavy metals from soils, so metal levels rise. Fish richness drops and dissolved oxygen does not increase, so only statement II is expected.

descriptor: Effective short-term remediation of the acidified pond.
solution: Adding calcium carbonate (liming) neutralizes the acid and raises pH quickly. Taller smokestacks move pollution elsewhere, and fertilizer controls address eutrophication, not acidity.

descriptor: Four-tank UV experiment on polar phytoplankton: which inference is supported by results.
solution: Photosynthesis was far higher when UV was filtered and fell when UV was added, so more UV through a thinner ozone layer would depress productivity further. The data do not address tropics, CFC causes or future UV levels.

descriptor: Most valid conclusion that can be inferred from the UV experiment.
solution: The results show UV strongly limits phytoplankton productivity, so ozone thinning could affect the base of the polar food web. Other options claim things the experiment did not test.

descriptor: Which two-tank comparison best shows natural-level UV inhibits photosynthesis.
solution: Tank 1 has natural UV and tank 2 has none. The large increase when UV is removed isolates the effect of natural UV.

descriptor: What would most add to the reliability of the experiment series.
solution: Reliability means repeatability, so repeating under identical conditions with similar results is the strongest support. Different conditions or more variables test generality or add new questions instead.

descriptor: Most likely effect of acid deposition on a northern forest.
solution: Acid deposition leaches nutrients and damages needles, so trees are weakened and tolerate cold less well. It increases hydrogen ions and lowers soil buffering, the reverse of the other options.

descriptor: Effluent chromium limits and a company discharging 32 ppm since 1981: which statement is correct.
solution: The limit was 37 ppm until 1986, so 32 ppm was legal through 1985. After the limit fell to 25 ppm, 32 ppm exceeded it, so a violation occurred later. The 1994 risk finding did not change the legal limit.
notes: Regulatory timeline reasoning; no matching CED topic.

descriptor: Doubling time for a population growing 1.75 percent a year.
solution: Rule of 70: 70 ÷ 1.75 = 40 years. Dividing 70 by the percent growth rate is the standard shortcut for doubling time, so the other values correspond to different growth rates.

descriptor: Which statements about ozone are true (acid-rain precursor, harmful, absorbs UV).
solution: Ground-level ozone harms lungs and stratospheric ozone absorbs some ultraviolet radiation. Ozone is not a precursor of acid rain, so only II and III are true.

descriptor: Where is danger from radon greatest.
solution: Radon seeps from soil and rock into buildings and accumulates where ventilation is limited. Tightly insulated homes trap it indoors.

descriptor: Why do most plastics pose a special problem in the waste stream.
solution: Plastics break down very slowly, if at all, so they persist in landfills and the environment. They do not readily release methane, ozone or radioactive isotopes.

descriptor: Which air pollutant is correctly paired with a major effect.
solution: Sulfur oxides react with water in the atmosphere to form sulfuric acid, causing acid deposition. The other pairings are mismatched.

descriptor: Which activity has a health risk most likely overestimated by the US public.
solution: People tend to overestimate unfamiliar, involuntary, dramatic risks such as nuclear plant accidents and underestimate familiar ones like driving or smoking.
notes: Risk perception is not itemized in the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Which is a primary air pollutant produced by burning coal.
solution: Primary pollutants are emitted directly, and incomplete combustion releases carbon monoxide. Ozone and sulfuric acid are secondary, formed later in the atmosphere.

descriptor: Farmer needs increasing pesticide concentrations to control a pest; best explanation.
solution: Insects with inherited resistance survive and reproduce, so resistance spreads through the population by natural selection. Acquired traits are not inherited.

descriptor: Fuel-source graph (1850-2000): year coal's share was greatest.
solution: In the graph the coal curve peaks near 1910, higher than at the other listed years. The 1880 and 1940 values are lower, and by 1970 and 2000 oil, gas and other sources had taken over.

descriptor: Same graph: approximate year oil and gas became dominant.
solution: The oil-and-gas curve crosses above coal around 1940. Before that, coal supplied the larger share, so earlier years do not fit.

descriptor: Why nuclear power cannot fully replace oil and gas.
solution: Nuclear plants produce electricity, but oil is also needed for transportation fuels and petrochemicals that electricity does not directly replace. The other options exaggerate or misstate facts.

descriptor: Primary cause of the decline in wood fuel in the 1800s.
solution: Widespread deforestation reduced wood supply, and coal became the replacement. Oil fields and warming did not cause the decline. Coal's energy density is actually higher than wood's, so option E is reversed.

descriptor: True statement about the stratosphere.
solution: The stratosphere contains the ozone layer, the highest natural ozone concentration. Weather and most water vapor lie in the troposphere.

descriptor: How is the crude growth rate r calculated.
solution: Growth rate equals birth rate minus death rate, ignoring migration. Multiplying by life expectancy or adding the rates would not give a rate of natural change.

descriptor: Most important factor in tree decline in northeastern US.
solution: Acid deposition mobilizes toxic metals such as aluminum in soil that harm roots, along with nutrient leaching. The other options are not the main factor.

descriptor: Which characteristically produces non-point-source pollution.
solution: Erosion and runoff from farmland come from a broad area with no single outlet. Landfill seepage, effluent pipes and sewage overflow are point sources. Point sources, by contrast, discharge through an identifiable pipe or leak.

descriptor: Global population graph to 2150: what will it most likely do.
solution: Reading the graph, population is about 5 billion in 1950 and near 10 billion by 2150, which is a doubling. It levels off rather than declining or growing exponentially.

descriptor: Factors increasing spread of infectious disease, EXCEPT which one.
solution: Neurotoxin exposure affects nervous or endocrine function and does not spread infection. Flooding, warming, insect vectors and urban crowding all do.

descriptor: Forest fires may emit up to 40 percent of annual global emissions of which gas.
solution: Burning biomass releases CO2 as the main carbon-containing product. Water vapor and ozone are not the main products of burning plant material.

descriptor: Which does NOT exert a major influence on Earth's overall climate.
solution: Solar input, atmospheric gases, land-ocean distribution and Earth's rotation and orbit shape global climate. Seasonal temperature inversions are local weather phenomena.

descriptor: Why does salmon farming threaten wild salmon.
solution: Dense pens concentrate parasites and disease that spread to passing wild fish. The other options misstate the main threat.

descriptor: Characteristic of r-selected species.
solution: R-selected species mature quickly and produce many offspring with little parental care. These traits suit unstable habitats and match rapid-colonizer strategies, the opposite of slow growth and long lives.

descriptor: Why biological control of insects is effective.
solution: Biological control usually targets one pest and the control organism can persist. It does not promote resistance and a pest explosion.

descriptor: Best example of an economic incentive.
solution: Tax breaks reward companies for using recycled materials, an incentive. Fees and taxes are disincentives.
notes: Economic policy tools are not in the 2026 CED topic list.

descriptor: How West Nile virus is acquired.
solution: It is spread by bites from infected mosquitoes. It is not acquired from food, water or direct contact with sick animals.

descriptor: Primary characteristic grasslands share.
solution: Seasonal temperature and rainfall cycles support abundant grass growth. Neither deserts nor forests share this pattern, and the 30° latitude limit and overgrazing statements are incorrect.

descriptor: What a cost-benefit analysis of a mine takes into account.
solution: It weighs all costs and benefits, including injury costs, restoration costs and the ore's value.
notes: Cost-benefit analysis is not itemized in the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Bar graph of precipitation pH: how many times more acidic NE US than South Pacific.
solution: pH 4.4 versus 5.4 differ by one unit, and each pH unit is a factor of ten in hydrogen ion concentration. Hydrogen ion concentration ratio = 10^(5.4 − 4.4) = 10.

descriptor: Primary cause of acid precipitation in northeastern US.
solution: Burning sulfur-containing fossil fuels, especially coal for electricity, releases SO2 that forms sulfuric acid.

descriptor: Which ecological concept includes all the others.
solution: An ecosystem includes the community and its abiotic environment, which in turn contains populations and species. Genus, species and population are all parts of a community, which is part of an ecosystem.

descriptor: Significant limitation of rat tests for cancer risk.
solution: Animal models may not reflect human responses. Differences in metabolism and body size between rats and people make extrapolation uncertain.

descriptor: Most successful solution to fish mortality caused by dams.
solution: Fish ladders allow fish to pass the dam. Repellents, harvesting before the dam or dredging do not let migrating fish move past the barrier.

descriptor: Action most likely to protect ecological systems in national forests.
solution: Selling logging rights at fair market value removes below-cost subsidies, so logging is less profitable.
notes: Federal forest policy is outside the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Soil sample passes 98 of 100 ml of water; which composition is likely.
solution: Mostly sand drains fastest because it has large pores.

descriptor: Which soil property most influences water flow through the sample.
solution: Permeability describes how easily water moves. Color, pH, salinity and fertility do not control how fast water moves.

descriptor: Anchovy catch table: low 1998 catch most likely from what.
solution: In 1998 the surface was very warm, indicating weakened upwelling that carries nutrients up, so productivity and catch fell.

descriptor: Cause of high 1998 sea surface temperature.
solution: El Niño brings warm water to the Peruvian coast. It is a recurring warm-water event in the equatorial Pacific, unlike eutrophication or salinization.

descriptor: Which is an example of an external cost.
solution: A cost borne by third parties not part of the transaction, such as medical bills from plant pollution.
notes: Economic concept not in the 2026 CED.

descriptor: Best representation of worldwide water use by sector.
solution: Agriculture uses about 70 percent, industry about 20 percent and domestic uses about 10 percent.

descriptor: Why native pollinators serve native plants better than honeybees.
solution: Native pollinators coevolved with native plants.

descriptor: Which best describes leaching.
solution: Leaching is water moving down through soil, dissolving and carrying material away. It is different from erosion, which moves soil particles, and from precipitation.

descriptor: Problem best addressed by contour plowing.
solution: Plowing along contours slows runoff and reduces soil erosion. It does not address nutrient or salt problems directly.

descriptor: Best example of cogeneration.
solution: Cogeneration captures waste heat from electricity production for another use such as heating. Using one plant to supply both electricity and heat raises overall energy efficiency.

descriptor: Correct pairing of agricultural practice and consequence.
solution: Flooded rice paddies are anaerobic and release methane.

descriptor: Why small island populations are prone to extinction.
solution: Small populations are vulnerable to unpredictable events such as storms or disease and have low genetic diversity. Larger or generalist populations are buffered, which is the opposite of what the other options claim.

descriptor: Which stratospheric substance increases albedo by reflecting sunlight.
solution: Sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight back to space, cooling Earth.

orig_ref: a693d29c-2010Intl, Sec II booklet p.2-3 (PDF p.36-37), FRQ 1
descriptor: News-article scenario on local toxic pollutants (PCBs, mercury, lead): source, exposure route and health effect, two control steps, child susceptibility, CO2 capture cost calculation, coal-plant emission control technology, reasons for offshoring manufacturing.
solution:
(a) Choose lead as the pollutant. (i) A source other than the chemical plants: old paint or lead water pipes. *(1 point: one specific source.)* (ii) Entry: children swallow paint chips or dust, or drink water that has passed through lead plumbing. Effect: lead damages the developing nervous system and lowers learning ability. *(2 points: 1 for the route, 1 for the health effect.)* (iii) Two steps short of a ban: set and enforce limits on lead in drinking water and replace old pipes; test and remove lead-based paint from older housing. Public education on avoiding exposure would also earn credit. *(2 points: 1 per specific step.)*
(b) Children take in more food, water and air per kilogram of body weight, and their growing organ systems are more sensitive than adult ones. *(1 point: one valid reason.)*
(c) Cost = 40 kg CO₂ × $0.75 per kg = $30 per MP3 player. *(2 points: 1 for the setup, 1 for the answer.)*
(d) Choose sulfur oxides: a flue-gas scrubber removes SO₂ from the exhaust. Alternatives are electrostatic precipitators or baghouse filters for particulates, and selective catalytic reduction for NOₓ. *(1 point: a technology matched to the pollutant.)*
(e) Two reasons: labor is cheaper, and environmental or workplace regulations are less strict or less strictly enforced, which lowers compliance costs. Other accepted reasons are cheaper land, lower taxes and access to large markets. *(2 points: 1 per reason, with brief discussion.)*
notes: Printed part points total 11 (1+2+2+1+2+1+2); the scoring worksheet caps the question at 10. The newspaper article figure is not reproduced; the three pollutants are named in the question text.

orig_ref: a693d29c-2010Intl, Sec II booklet p.4 (PDF p.38), FRQ 2
descriptor: Termite wood-consumption table by temperature and humidity: find optimum, scale methane emissions over a forest area and under a warmer, drier scenario, explain population limits, post-clearing density boom and bust, and another climate effect of deforestation.
solution:
(a)(i) Highest consumption in the table is 0.27 mg per day per termite, at 30 °C and 90% relative humidity. *(1 point: both values.)*
(ii) CH₄ = 2,000 ha × 4.5 × 10⁷ termites/ha × 70 kg CH₄ per year per 1,000 termites = 6.3 × 10⁹ kg CH₄ per year. *(2 points: 1 for setup with units, 1 for the answer.)*
(iii) At 35 °C and 50% humidity consumption is 0.09, so emissions scale by 0.09/0.27 = one third: 6.3 × 10⁹ × 0.09/0.27 = 2.1 × 10⁹ kg CH₄ per year. *(2 points: 1 for setup, 1 for the answer.)*
(iv) Temperature and humidity are limiting factors with a range of tolerance. At 40 °C consumption stops, so termites and their gut microbes likely die; outside the tolerance range, reproduction and colony founding fall, so population size falls. *(2 points: 1 for the reason, 1 for the linked explanation.)*
(b)(i) Clearing leaves a large amount of dead wood and plant material, which raises food supply and supports more termites. *(1 point.)* (ii) The extra food is used up, the population exceeds carrying capacity and crashes; loss of shade also raises surface temperature beyond termite tolerance. *(1 point.)*
(c) Removing trees reduces photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is taken up and the carbon sink is lost; burning cleared trees also releases CO₂. *(2 points: 1 for the change, 1 for the climate link.)*
notes: Printed part points total 11; the worksheet caps the question at 10. Table values read from the printed text layer and consistent with guideline answers.

orig_ref: a693d29c-2010Intl, Sec II booklet p.5 (PDF p.39), FRQ 3
descriptor: Zebra mussel invasion in the Great Lakes with a range map: why mainly eastern, how lakes get colonized and one prevention method, an ecosystem impact, another invasive species, a biological-control example with its downside, and two traits that favor invaders.
solution:
(a) The mussels were introduced in the East and are still spreading west; the Rocky Mountains and scarcer connected waters in the West slow their spread, and boating traffic is denser in the East. *(1 point: one valid explanation.)*
(b) Mussels hitch rides on boat hulls and trailers or in bilge and bait water, and they move on waterfowl. Prevention: require inspection, cleaning and draining of boats before they enter a new lake. *(2 points: 1 for a mechanism, 1 for a prevention method.)*
(c) Zebra mussels filter plankton from the water, which increases water clarity; more light reaches the bottom and aquatic plants grow more, while competition for plankton reduces native mollusks and zooplankton feeders. *(2 points: 1 for the impact, 1 for the linked explanation.)*
(d) Kudzu vine smothers and shades out native plants. Other accepted: emerald ash borer, which kills ash trees. *(2 points: 1 for the species, 1 for the impact.)*
(e) Example: the cane toad was introduced to control beetle pests; it became invasive itself and poisoned native predators that ate it. *(2 points: 1 for a real example, 1 for a negative impact.)*
(f) Two traits: a high reproductive rate (many offspring, early maturity) and generalist habits or strong dispersal, so they can use many foods and habitats and spread quickly. *(2 points: 1 per trait.)*
notes: Printed part points total 11; the worksheet caps the question at 10. Range map not reproduced.

orig_ref: a693d29c-2010Intl, Sec II booklet p.6 (PDF p.40), FRQ 4
descriptor: Sea-level rise tied to warming at 3.0 mm per year: calculate rise over 50 years, two warming processes that raise sea level, two estuary impacts, one economic loss for coastal residents, two policies to discourage coastal settlement.
solution:
(a) Rise = 3.0 mm/yr × 50 yr = 150 mm = 0.15 m. *(2 points: 1 for the setup, 1 for the answer.)*
(b) First: melting of land-based ice such as the Greenland ice sheet or mountain glaciers adds water to the ocean. Second: thermal expansion, because warmer water has greater volume. *(4 points: 1 for each process, 1 for each explanation.)* Floating sea ice does not raise sea level when it melts.
(c) Two impacts: flooding converts marshes and mangroves to open water, removing nursery habitat for fish and shellfish; saltwater moves farther inland, changing salinity and eliminating species with narrow salt tolerance. Loss of the buffer also raises storm damage inland. *(2 points: 1 per impact.)*
(d)(i) Rising seas damage or destroy property, lowering property values and raising insurance and repair costs. *(1 point.)* (ii) Two strategies: raise insurance premiums or deny coverage in repeatedly flooded areas; zone to restrict new building near the shore. Ending subsidies for beach protection is another option. *(2 points: 1 per strategy.)*
notes: Printed part points total 11; the worksheet caps the question at 10.
